utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There is still a motion pending on protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the Chamber is inclined to give the parties an opportunity to put further questions in relation to that motion to the witness and will then give its ruling on the matter. But that should be done in closed session. Therefore, we turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to examine Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. President, whether the witness's full name was recorded previously. No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not before we entered into closed session, and I didn't -- you didn't ask her, as a matter of fact, the parties didn't ask her to state her full name for the record, so that still should be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maria Teresa Mauro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you provide two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor on 2nd and 3rd March, 2000, and for the second time on 5th and 6th January, 2008?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And since then, have you had an opportunity to examine both those statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you find that the contents of the two statements accurately reflected what you stated to the members of the Office of the Prosecutor on those previous occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call for document number 5362, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the document will come up on the screen in front of you, Ms. Mauro. While that's happening, if you could say, are the contents of both those statements true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you were asked the questions that were asked of you by the members of the Office of the Prosecutor in March 2000 and in January 2008 again today in court, would your responses be the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could just -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you identify that as your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar, can we take the document -- the English version to the -- not the last page. The one before the last page, the signature page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the written submissions, I take it that there are no objections against admission. Mr. Registrar, the 2000 statement would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number P1098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the 2008 statement would be ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me call that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We have not seen it. Yes. I'm too early. P1098 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could bring up on the screen document 5362, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Ms. Mauro, if you could look at the next document that comes up on the screen and identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any problem as far as the number is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 5363, Mr. Registrar. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, is that your document of 2008?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I move this statement into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same observation, as far as Defence submissions are concerned. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1099, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1099 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, how will we deal, because we have one related exhibit still to be added to the 65 ter list - I do understand that's one HRAT report - in addition to the ones that were already on the 65 ter list. I do understand that there's no objection against adding that to the 65 ter list. The other related exhibits, will you put them on the list and that we --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will call up only three documents of that list at the end of the session, so we will provide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then the remainder we'll find on a list so that Mr. Registrar can assign numbers to those you did not refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, at the time you provided the supplemental statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2008, did you examine a number of reports, majority of which were authored or co-authored by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you examine those documents since 2008, since the time you made the supplementary statement, particularly on Sunday or yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that the contents of those documents are true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I read the summary of the witness's 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. You have explained to the witness what the purpose of reading out the summary is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Maria Teresa Mauro worked as an UN civil affairs officer based in Knin from March to December 1995. She was present during the shelling of Knin on 4th and 5th August, 1995. She was a member of the Human Rights Action Team, known as HRAT, from 7 August 1995, and in this capacity conducted daily HRAT patrols in the southern Krajina. She reported on her observations and compiled a number of HRAT reports containing information of human rights violations observed by HRAT monitors during and in the aftermath of Operation Storm. Ms. Mauro provided direct notice of crimes to accused Ivan Cermak. That is all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the witness could be handed over the hard copies of the statement and -- thank you, Madam Usher. And, Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit P1098 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, if you could look at your 2000 statement, and you have the hard copies before you. You can peruse them or follow it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could move to page 3 on the English translation, the original, and page 3 of the Croatian version. The paragraphs are not numbered but paragraph 3 on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say -- this is what you say: "I can remember General Cermak arriving early on after the attack and often being available to talk about the problems that we encountered. He appeared to be the main authority in the area and had a number of aides with him. Cermak wore a uniform and was apparently the governor of Knin at that time." Now my question to you, Ms. Mauro, is: What were the factors that led you to think that Mr. Cermak appeared to be the main authority in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was the person that also others were referring to when situations were difficult and needed to be taken care of and resolved, and it was obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you be a little bit more specific, Ms. Mauro, when you say it was obvious. Apart from others referring to, did you observe anything personally which led you to conclude that Mr. Cermak was the main authority in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was the most senior -- it is undoubtful because also within our own hierarchy, the person that we were relating to was him, and I referred to General Forand or the head of my office, so the highest authority in the area was him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As I understood you, you said: "Within our own hierarchy, the person we were relating to was him..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I see. And now, in your statement you talk about having personal contact with him, participating in meetings with him. What were your personal observations about the particular meetings and how Mr. Cermak expressed himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's exactly what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins. One second.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is to the way that the question was put by Ms. Mahindaratne whereby she states -- she refers to: "You talk about having personal contact with him, participating in meetings with him." In my submission, we must take care at this point, and there must be a basis put as to whether or not that is accurate and the nature of any contact that this witness had, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I can refer the paragraphs in the statement. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the statement, of course, there is some mention of direct contact. Whether we call it a meeting or did you meet someone not in a meeting, that's -- but in -- I do understand that your question relates to direct contact between this witness and Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please, then, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question, Ms. Mauro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In your personal direct contact with Mr. Cermak, how did you see or understand Mr. Cermak's authority in the area to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is exactly as I wrote in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And could you express that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the authority in the area. He was the person we would refer to when there were issues to be looked at, and situations which were difficult were addressed to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I would go to those issues and situations in a moment. But before going on to that, when you address particular matters with Mr. Cermak, at any time did he ever inform you that you should address those matters with someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And let me take you to paragraph 5 of your 2008 statement, Ms. Mauro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could have P1099 on the screen. If we could have page 2 of the statement -- that is, page 3, that is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, at paragraph 5 of your 2008 statement, you say: "In page 3 of my previous statement, paragraph 3 and 4, I refer to General Cermak and his aides being notified of the crimes and their responses. On some occasions, I have personally spoken with General Cermak in the UN compound, and I have informed him of the situation." Now, could you be specific? What did you refer to as the situation? What exactly did you inform Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plight of the very few people remaining in the area and the difficulties of the very sparse and isolated remaining population in the sector known then as Sector South, and there are difficulties to cope with surviving and the problems of arson and the problems of livelihood and looting and robbing and harassment and crimes which people had witnessed or were aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And -- well, you say in that same paragraph: "On these occasions, he seemed willing to cooperate and always assured that the matter will be looked into and that he wanted to be informed about criminal activities, if any. General Cermak always assured us that the situation was under control." Now, at those times you addressed these matters with General Cermak and he assured you that the matter was under control, did it seem to you that, in fact, that was, indeed, the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It was a leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see any leading aspect of it. You know, I asked a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although there is some leading element, it's not inappropriate to put a question in this way. The question has been answered. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And after these conversations with Mr. Cermak, was something done about the -- these issues that you raised with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you read my reports, it doesn't look like other reports of other HRAT teams. The situation deteriorated until when we left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that question. Now, let me take you to paragraph 6 of your 2008 statement, Ms. Mauro, where you say: "Following one of these conversations with General Cermak, a few days later while on patrol, we observed crimes being committed (arson). We immediately returned to Knin and informed General Cermak's office, providing precise coordinates on where this crime was happening. The aide for General Cermak assured us that the matter would be looked upon -- looked, upon which we returned to the UN camp and informed General Forand." Now, did you ever receive any information after that report was made to General Cermak's office, that that particular incident where you provided coordinates to General Cermak's aide had been investigated into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I recall correctly, at this -- in this period, the start of the denial-type of attitude. In other words, we were not saying the truth, according to the Croatian authority we were informing of and General Cermak as well. So from the population, no, I did not understand that that action had been taken to alleviate the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your answer is, you say: "Well, if I recall correctly at this -- in this period, the..." There was a "denial-type of attitude. In other words, we were not saying the truth, according to the Croatian authority we were informing of and General Cermak as well." Now, can you -- are you able to specifically refer to a particular instance when General Cermak, you know, expressed this type of denial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There should be a letter where he expressed this type of denial.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have P36 on the screen, please. And if we can go to the next page, Mr. Registrar, and if you could just focus on -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, I'd like to you look at this document. In fact, you have referred to this document at paragraph 41 of your 2008 statement. This is an HRAT report compiled by you and Mr. Edward Flynn. In paragraph -- the second paragraph under paragraph number 2, that is, in fact, paragraph 3, you -- it's reported, it says: "The Croatian civilian police presence in the areas outside the main towns remain almost non-existent. The resulting freedom this gives to roving gangs of uniformed Croatian soldiers who loot and burn at will has placed the few remaining residents of the countryside in Sector South in a virtually continual state of fear. This situation provides a marked contrast to the picture proffered by Military Governor Cermak, who insisted in a letter dated 3rd September to Sector Commander Forand ... that he is astonished at your statements about persecution of the poor and miserable from their land." Is that the letter you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "General Cermak stated his full willingness to visit personally sites where abuses are observed by the UN, but today when yet another was observed (following paragraph) General Cermak was out of town." And in the following paragraph: "The incident is referred to" --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could just bring up -- focus on the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- "to the 4th September. An HRAT visited hamlets of Tintori, Petrovici, and Cvijanovici" -- pardon my pronunciation -- "in the Plavno valley, 20 kilometres north of Knin. Residents of all villages reported a weekend replete with fear caused by roving gangs of uniformed Croatian soldiers." And -- there are details of the incident. A few lines below -- it says: "On returning, they surprised two uniformed soldiers of the 4th Split brigade lounging next to a burning house." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "A second building was seen burning just up the hill. The soldiers spoke vaguely of some other soldiers setting the blazes." Now, according to this report, it says in the previous paragraph that when this particular incident was observed, General Cermak was out of town. Now, can you explain it, is it -- what is the connection about this incident and General Cermak being out of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because I was advised -- we reported the incident when we came from this area. We passed by the office of General Cermak in Knin, and we informed them that this had happened. But we were told that he was out of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you -- to whom did you provide that information? Was it an official of the office or just a person there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was an official of the office. I don't recall the name. I don't recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And consequent to that report, did you -- were you informed that an investigation has been carried out into that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have P46 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And while that document is being brought up, Ms. Mauro, if I could ask you to look at paragraph 33 of your 2008 statement where you refer to the HRAT report for 22nd August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in this report, it's recorded of a meeting between you and the chief of Knin, Mr. Romanic. Who else was present at this meeting, that is, the meeting between you and Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, there was an interpreter, and most probably both the UN CIVPOL and the UNMO were in the room with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this report also refers to a meeting with Mr. Jukic, Pavo, the office in charge of civil Defence in Knin. Now was this meeting taken together with Mr. Romanic and Mr. Pavo Jukic, or were they two separate meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was the purpose of this meeting? I'm sorry. It's already said: To address the concerns of security and safety for the remaining population in the Plavno area. Can you say, what exactly did you inform Mr. Romanic as being the issue of security and safety for the inhabitants of the Plavno area? What were the inhabitants facing at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, eventually, when we went to the Plavno area for the first time, it was quite an isolated area, and the road to get there was quite difficult. And the first time we went there, the people was absolutely frightened, and we found devastation all over, and also, so many animals who were lying in the fields, and only older [Realtime transcript read in error, "all the"] people had remained, and we were told about dead bodies buried, not buried, and no electricity, no utilities whatsoever. So we thought that we could draw the attention of the Croatian authority on this situation because essentially everybody wanted to leave, and we asked -- we went back to Knin, and we set up this meeting with Mr. Romanic with the idea that we would have a meeting with the remaining population together the day after or as soon as he was available so that we could reassure and find a way to appease their plight. And so we set up this meeting, and -- well, the story is another one, but this is the reason why I was there, and with Mr. -- civil defence. It was to discuss about the various burial sites which we had visited and to understand whether they had a clear idea on who was buried and where and why and identification, if there was a central database for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, just for the record. You said only the older people had remained, because it reads "all the people," which is, of course, from hearing almost the same. Only the older people had remained. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did the -- did you have communication? Did you speak with the remaining inhabitants of the Plavno area before this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did they indicate to you why they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were fearing for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I just wanted to go back and ask a question that I should have asked you before. You mentioned an interpreter present at your meetings with Mr. Romanic. When you communicated with Mr. Cermak, did you communicate through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And whose interpreter was that? Was it a UN interpreter or Mr. Cermak's interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UN interpreter was always with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did Mr. Cermak have his own interpreter at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes, but we didn't use in our communication, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 1824, please. And if we can -- Mr. Registrar, if we could move to page 2. I'm sorry. It should be page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, this is one of your HRAT reports that you referred to in your 2008 statement. If you could look at that last paragraph. It's reported as this: "On the same day, the HRAT met Mr. Barisic, Milan, Ministry of Interior coordinator for Gracac area. Mr. Barisic expressed his appreciation for the good cooperation established with the international organisations so far. He stated that Croatian police was trying to do its utmost to guarantee the safety of the Serb population remaining. However, he emphasised that it was difficult to control the 200 square kilometre under the jurisdiction of Gracac police station. "According to Mr. Barisic, the Croatian police, for security reasons, refrains from patrolling the border side with Bosnia and the southern part (in Knin direction) of Gracac AOR. In the southern part, a number of individuals, former HV soldiers and thus wearing uniforms, are undertaking criminal actions and are particularly aggressive. Up to now, the concerned authorities brought charges against 30 to 35 of them. However, for looting activities, the perpetrators are not supposed to be taken into custody. Mr. Barisic could not specify which kind of charges were brought against those criminals." Now, my first question to you is: Was Mr. Barisic a uniformed policeman or an official from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember how -- what was he dressing then, what was he wearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where did you meet him? At his office in Gracac or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was there -- who introduced Mr. Barisic as the coordinator for the Ministry of Interior for Gracac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And it's reported here that he said that: "... for looting activities, the perpetrators are not supposed to be taken into custody." Now, what did you understand that statement to be? You reported it. Well, how did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was tolerated, looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you ask him what the basis for that decision was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him, So what kind of charges would eventually be brought against these criminals?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what was his response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No response. Otherwise, would have been written.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you tell him -- did he inform you as to who had given such instructions as to not taking perpetrators of looting activity into custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask. But he was representative of Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I move this document into evidence, please. It's included in the 92 ter submission. I'll have it removed from the lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit number P1100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P1100 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have document number 3062, please. Mr. President, this document from page 4 onwards has a chart, which has already -- the chart has been tendered into evidence already under Exhibit number P688. However, for the time being, I left the chart there so that I could demonstrate that this summary at page 1 to 3 is based on the chart, but we will remove the chart and just -- I will only tender the first three pages into evidence later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a compilation of dead bodies, crimes involving death, which either the UN personnel or the civilian population would bring to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at your 2008 statement, paragraph 57, 58 and 59 where you refer to this list. And paragraph 58, you say -- with regard to the people who were responsible for compiling this report, you say: "A team comprising of Sajin Zhang, myself, Judith Jacob and the interpreter was responsible for compiling this data." Now, was Mr. Judith Jacob Mr. Alun Roberts's secretary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, it was an assistant. She was working the PIO session, public information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to submit page 1, 2, 3, of this document into evidence. I'll have the rest of the pages removed from e-court later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P1101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P1101 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, may I call document 2854 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an analysis of the situation of the refugees who were to come mainly from the last exodus from Krajina in the former Yugoslavia and then in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia still.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where were you based at when you compiled this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was based at the office in Belgrade of the UN office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In compiling this report, what type of research did you carry out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I spoke with the United Nations high commissioner for refugees; I spoke with the Serbian office for refugees and IDP; and I spoke with some -- Helsinki Committee, some non-governmental organisations, including the Helsinki Committee. Mainly, these were the main sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Ms. Mahindaratne please switch off the mic while the witness is answering because it's very difficult to hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in carrying out that research, did you receive any information as to the willingness of the Serb refugees who were in the FRY and Serbia and who had left Krajina --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- to return to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did receive, also, information from former inhabitants of Krajina, but the information they had concerning the overall situation back home was so difficult that nobody really was thinking to go back except for trying to recuperate some of their belongings or their property or to some assist some of the elderly that had remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say "... information they had concerning the overall situation back home was so difficult that nobody really was thinking to go back..." Now, can you be more specific and clarify what you meant by "so difficult"? What exactly -- what type of information were they receiving?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. If we could get more foundation as to the source of this information in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The witness just testified that she did have information coming from the inhabitants, previous answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many, who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- apparently, the witness received information about that. Could you tell us from whom you received that information about that being difficult, how many people you spoke about that, and whether they gave any further details about the difficulties they thought would be there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, besides the people, the number of the people I spoke with originating from that area, I don't remember, but I am certain that my former landlady was in Belgrade with all her family and all her relatives, and there were approximately 20, 30 people if we look at the extended family. But then there were also the interpreters. Some of them had remained in the area; not all of them moved out of Sector South. So they were also a source of information, and there were also other interpreters who instead had come along, and there were people whom I had met during my period in Krajina, and there was also difficulties for the UNHCR to organise this visit and -- and related to the information they were receiving. So it was -- it was -- it was an open secret.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you -- when you said it was difficult for the UNHCR to organise this visit, what were you referring to? Visit to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because at a certain stage there was this idea that the UNHCR would help people to go and visit the area with an intention to facilitate the return. But there were also difficulties to obtain authorisation from the Croatian relevant authorities to -- to undertake these visits. So there were two -- two camps of obstruction for the return, if you wish to -- one was the current situation on the ground, and the other was the reluctance of the Croatian authorities to facilitate going to see, visit, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Ms. Mahindaratne invited you to describe the difficulties, which you say now part of it was the current situation on the ground. Could you give us further information about what the situation on the ground was so that they did not think of returning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So infrastructure were not restored for a long time. The houses had been destroyed and were still destroyed. The livelihood, which for many of them were animals and cattle, had been either killed or either stolen. The belongings of the people were not in the house anymore. My own residence was looted, just as an example. So harassment was still ongoing, and we were hearing about, still, cleaning-up operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when was it that you compiled this report? And when you're referring to being in Belgrade getting this information, what period was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- it is written in the report, is 6 June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mauro, for responding to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that -- if I may tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P1102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1102 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Yes. The cleaning-up operations you talked about, did you still receive reports on that in June 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally didn't receive a report, but I heard information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was that up-to-date information on what happened in, well, let's say, May, June, 1996, or would that refer to an earlier period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't specify that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, you're already on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wonder if Your Honour would contemplate taking the break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that would be a good idea, that we have an early break and that you will be cross-examined after the break. We will have a break, and we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, I'm going ask you some questions on behalf of Mr. Cermak, and I'd like to start with your job and the reporting mechanism back between March to December 1995. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we know that you worked in Knin as a civil affairs officer from March to December 1995. Can you tell me who your superior in Knin was, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Previously, before Al-Alfi, Mr. Al-Alfi was Mr. Amir Kotnik [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And is it correct that in your position you were involved in the daily patrols in and around the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, after you patrolled together with your colleagues, you would then be involved in the preparation of daily reports on behalf of HRAT. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the HRAT didn't start up to August.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let's take it from the 7th of August onwards, if we may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So from that time, you were involved in the preparation of daily reports. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to make a pause between when you and I answer each other just for the purpose of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just so that we understand as clearly as possible, during your work as a member of a HRAT team, how many people were in each HRAT patrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally was an UN CIVPOL and UNMO and an interpreter. And at times, we joined with the civil affairs -- sorry, the UN human rights officer, and occasionally the UNHCR officers were also coming with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So between four to six people in reach HRAT? Would that be approximately correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the usual composition was a UN civil affairs, a UN CIVPOL, and a military observer and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. On average, how many HRAT teams were patrolling at any one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depended, because we didn't receive the additional staff, but at the beginning we were three.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And is it right that all team members after they had come back from the patrols would then have a debriefing session in Mr. Al-Alfi's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And he, just for the record, was a civil affairs coordinator. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And is it also right that all the HRAT teams who had been out that day, however composed, would take part in those debriefings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally would be the civil affairs officers, all of them, and the head of the departments, UNMO, or CIVPOL, not all the CIVPOL who were with us or not all the UNMOs who were with us, but UNHCR as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: How many people might have input during those debriefing sessions into providing information for the reports that were produced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, everybody had an input on what they had observed during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And how many people -- can you tell me an approximation of how many might be at that debriefing meeting, given the number of teams and the people involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Coordinator; deputy; human rights office; and we were three civil affairs officers; plus we had the head of UNMO; the head of CIVPOL; military were also present from the General Forand's office; and UNHCR; and then at a later stage, also, the ECMM were with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And again, just so that I understand, would the purpose of those debriefing sessions be effectively to pool the information that you had and a report, a single report be produced, or were there a number of reports produced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended. Generally, there was a single report, but sometimes there were cumulative reports, but I needed to specify that we had a colleague covering the Korenica area, and he attended occasionally, not all the time. But he was providing reports and sending to us on daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Where would those reports be sent to, Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In terms of the debriefing session, would Mr. Flynn often attend those sessions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Always, when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And what about General Forand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes. But usually it was Colonel Leslie or someone else from General Forand's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you've clarified in your 2008 statement that the HRAT reports would, of course, include information from the UN components such as the UNMOs, the UN CIVPOL, and the UNHCR, details of which would be set out in the report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understand correctly your question, there is an misunderstanding, because the reports were compiled by the HRAT. At times, there were some information from UNHCR, but if you read, there are not so many at times. So it was the HRAT which was compiling the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, those HRAT reports also contained information about meetings that had been held between various UN officials, for example, Mr. Al-Alfi, General Forand, with local individuals such as Mr. Cermak. Is that a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some reference to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, during the course of your two statements that you have given to the Prosecution, you have been asked to review over 50 HRAT reports, most of which - it's fair to say - are evidence in this trial already, Ms. Mauro. Just, again, for the sake of clarity so I understand, is it right that having gone through those reports, the aspects that you were able to speak to and that you knew about from talking with others are the aspects that have you set out in your witness statement, where you comment upon those reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, actually, most of the reports are my own reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: A number of the reports are uninitialed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Show me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, I'll come back to that if I may. What I'm asking you is: Your knowledge of events, as I understand, Ms. Mauro, you're not saying that you had personal knowledge of everything contained in those reports; for example, some of the information would have been told to you by others evidently involved in the field elsewhere. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, in the sense that when we -- in part of the report I was always involved firsthand, if there is my initial there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, I'll come on to dealing with some of the reports in a moment. Let me just ask you now about Mr. Cermak's arrival and your contact with him. Again, you can take it from me or look at the statements before you, if you prefer. In your statement in 2000, at page 3, you say: "I can remember General Cermak arriving earlier on after the attack and often being available to talk about the problems that we encountered." And that paragraph was read out to you by Ms. Mahindaratne, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Were you aware or did you come to know at any stage that Mr. Cermak came to Knin on the 6th of August? Is that something that you came to know at some stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I saw him, if it was not 6, it was 7 or 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And during your stay in Knin and your interactions in the UN camp, did you also come to know early on that part of Mr. Cermak's function was to assist the UN in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, to assist the UN in Sector South, to -- I mean, our understanding was that he was there to assist the people in Sector South and to facilitate the UN work.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the facilitation of the UN work meant actually assisting with practical problems that the UN were facing, for example, the recovery of stolen vehicles. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were not really facing that problems in that period. We were, rather, trying to draw the attention of the authorities on the problems that the people were facing. That was our main function because we were totally aware that Croatia was an independent country.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You may not have been aware of the question of the UN stolen vehicles, but did you come to know that it was an issue for General Forand, for example, on which he corresponded with Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a political humanitarian officer there. I was not involved in security as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, the problems that we encountered, as you refer to, those problems obviously included the people who were within the UN camp from the area, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yeah. And the overall situation and those problems also included, would you agree, issues concerning normalisation of life post-Operation Storm, for example, the restoration of water, restoration of electricity. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Also, the workings of the hospital, the shops, the banks and commerce in and around Knin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, we know from your statement that you came across Mr. Cermak in the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Are you able to give me a date to assist me with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Early -- quite early in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you recall, for example, or did it come to your knowledge that Mr. Cermak was providing assistance to the displaced people in the camp by way of food, blankets, cigarettes? Did you come to know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, in any case, were not enough because we didn't even have food for ourselves because we were cut out of supplies.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know about the setting-up of a public kitchen, which was actually located in the garrison building to assist with provision of food to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess it came at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you come to know about that provision of food from the garrison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know who was providing that food.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, to go back to the wording of your statement, in 2008, you say at paragraph 5, so that you can follow if would you like to: "On some occasions, I have personally spoken with General Cermak in the UN compound, and I have informed him of the situation." Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You were asked in your examination-in-chief as to what you talked to Mr. Cermak about, and would it be fair to summarize in this way, that you talked to him about the problems that were persisting in the area and issues of general crime that was occurring, wasn't specific examples that you brought to his attention. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we also brought to him specific examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What were those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Plavno valley when it was burning, despite the assurances of the contrary, and other incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, that's the Grubori incident that you are talking about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And when did you provide notification to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went to his office, but he was out of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Was that on the 4th of September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Well, I should look into the reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, please do so, if you would care to take the opportunity so that we can be clear about it, because that's the occasion that you have told us about in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But we went already through this, right, where we informed him about an arson incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. There is -- let me take you, perhaps, to be of assistance, to your statement, where you recall providing specific reference --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is. Yes. You know, I should look -- because it's paragraph 6 in fact. But I should look into the report, the single individual report, and -- right? So you have in paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can you read paragraph 6 very carefully to yourself for a moment? Because I have a particular question that I'd like to ask you, so if can you just reread that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Done.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. The question is this: On rereading that paragraph, is that not in fact the incident of the burning that you came across in Grubori on the 25th of August that you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I finish my question, please, Ms. Mauro, that you came across and reported to the office, you say, of General Cermak. Is that not one and the same incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: How can you be so sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I remember that Grubori was a very long day for all of us, and I don't even remember that I was going to the office of Cermak myself, but I do remember that after Grubori, of course, we kept the Plavno under scrutiny, so we went back a few days later, and we had a similar incident. But there -- I'm certain there are reports about this other incident --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We'll come on to Grubori just so that you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: But this paragraph 6, you say that you informed General Cermak's office. Who was it in General Cermak's office that you informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were more people. There was one person who came to us, and we left -- the message, we left to the coordinator. Then we went to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you're not after this time able to give me the name of the individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can you give me a HRAT report in which this incident is recorded, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I? In fact, in examination-in-chief I called up document P36, which records the matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, you...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can you ask you this, Ms. Mauro: You've said there were several occasions on which specifics were given. You've drawn my attention to this one that you distinguish from Grubori. Can I ask you to provide me with any others, please, specific incidents that were reported to the office, as you say, of Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not through me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just wish to point out that there is another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what you're going to say, Ms. Mahindaratne. If there's any additional matter you'd like to raise, of course, then in re-examination you have opportunity to do that. I think where Ms. Higgins specifically asked whether there was a report and whether since this was dealt with in examination-in-chief, I think it was not inappropriate to point at P36. But we should refrain from intervening or interfering with the examination by the other party at loose grounds. So unless there's really something that you have thought over to be fully appropriate now to raise; otherwise, you should keep it for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let's go back to the UN camp, because I'm still interested in the contact that you had with Mr. Cermak. And let's go back, perhaps, to the 7th, and it may jog your memory, Ms. Mauro, and if we consider that as a matter of record that was the day on which the Akashi delegation arrived, something I know you recall from your 2000 statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I recall the day. I recall that the Akashi delegation arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Were you part of the group that spoke with Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I just saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you saw Mr. Cermak that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you spoke to him that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you come to hear through your debriefing sessions about Mr. Cermak's, as it was recorded, strong desire - words of Mr. Akashi - for all those people who were in the camp to stay in Knin and remain living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Going back to the incident of Mr. Akashi's delegation arriving, did it come to your attention through the debriefing sessions that it had been reported by Mr. Akashi that Mr. Cermak had a strong desire for those people in the camp to remain living in and around Knin from where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that two days, our priority was to get food, water, and freedom of movement because we were, in fact, not allowed to go anywhere, and we had no supplies, either, because we had finished them. Also, it was nearly finished because we were hosting a number of people who were not foreseen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, if I may stop you there. I do understand that you had other priorities at that moment, but Ms. Higgins specifically asked you whether you learned at any debriefing session about this wish, strong desire by Mr. Cermak for those living in the camp to remain living in and around Knin. Even though you may have had many others, perhaps, even for you, more pressing matters on your mind, that is what Ms. Higgins would like to know from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I remember we were discussing about Sarinic letter. That was one part, important part of the debriefing at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Were you in the UN camp on the 8th; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends what time and --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, let me try and orientate you by informing you that on that date, we have in fact a HRAT report, which records --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If I can have on the screen to assist P29, please, Mr. Registrar, second page at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: A report of Mr. Cermak addressing a committee of the dismissed persons at the compound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present at this -- this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just ask you this, whether through, again, the method and mechanism of the debriefing sessions that you had, did it come to your attention, if you see at the very bottom of that page the second line from the bottom: "Today, however, General Cermak came to the compound and in the UN's presence delivered to a committee of the DPs..."

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next page, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you can read it for yourself, Ms. Mauro. It concerns coming to convey the Croatian government's position concerning their reintegration and in a reassuring tone informing those displaced persons of the range of the rights that would be guaranteed to them in Knin and in the region which extended to citizenship, food, assistance, full employment, et cetera. You'll see there an observation that Mr. Cermak stressed that Croatia does not want a dead town and wishes for all these people to live there. Do you see that, and did it come to your attention either at the time or shortly thereafter that that was in fact the position that Mr. Cermak had put forward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, again, we know from the way that have you worded it in your statement that you recalled him coming to the UN compound to inquire about the situation there. Did you come to see, in fact, the document that was issued as a result of Mr. Cermak's address? And let me give you the opportunity of seeing that record.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It's D300, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, were you able to read Croatian at the time you were present in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you could just take a look at the English translation and see whether or not that was something that came to your attention, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the conversations that you had with Mr. Cermak, can you give me any indication of how many conversations you had with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And did all of those take place in the UN compound itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I know from your statement, again, in 2008, at page 3, that you refer to the fact that you recorded your observations at that time in an individual notebook. That's what you say in your statement, and please, again, feel free to take a look. It's page 3, paragraph 12. Do you still have your notebooks from that time, Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, unfortunately. But excuse me, which one you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Paragraph 12 of the 2008 statement. "During our patrols, we recorded our observations in our individual notebooks."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm interested in whether or not those are still in existence. No. Do you know what happened to your notebooks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Burned. Thrown away.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So the answer is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shredded.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shredded.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: They were shredded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you know when they were shredded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By ourselves. After we were compiling the notebook, when was it finished, usually we wouldn't keep because the information were recorded on the computer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any formal meeting with Mr. Cermak himself at the garrison building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you, as a patroller, ever request an official meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Why -- why not? Was there any particular reason why that wouldn't have been appropriate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, usually it was relating to General Forand and -- and Mr. Al-Alfi, so it was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the conversations, a couple of conversations that you had in the compound, presumably those were in the presence of other people who were there at the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyone else present during the conversations with Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, at page 2 of your 2008 statement, paragraph 5, you're referring to the occasions on which you spoke with him, and your observations were these: "On these occasions, he seemed willing to cooperate and always assured us that the matter will be looked into and that he wanted to be informed about criminal activities, if any ..." It's the paragraph that was read to you earlier. Do you see that, Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it right to say that from the brief contact that you had with Mr. Cermak in the UN compound that he was cooperative and trying to help out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. Is it fair to say that given your position in Knin at that time, you weren't privy to the knowledge of what resources he had available to him or what he was authorised to do? It's not something you knew about, was it, Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he seemed to the point of reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I understand that. My question is a bit more specific, in terms of whether you knew the resources he had available to him and whether you knew the authority he had to assist. Do you see the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The resources, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authority, I -- it was stated because he wanted to be informed and he wanted to -- and he was reassuring. He was saying that the situation was under control, so -- and others were -- I think also the chief of police referred to -- to General Cermak, like, I can't really, but General Cermak... So it was a point of reference, and he was very reassuring in his attitude.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: A point of reference, I don't disagree with you, Ms. Mauro. My question was centered more on whether or not, for example, you ever received or knew about in your position his terms of reference, what his actual function was in Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning there were no civilian authorities so he had a overall jurisdiction over the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence in chief, you told us that your assumptions about his authority were based on his contact with the Sector South chief or, effectively, the higher echelons of the hierarchy. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't have any other one to really relate to, except the chief of police, Romanic, in fact, for a while because then it was -- suddenly, he left.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. But in turn, you have said that he had overall jurisdiction over the area. Ms. Mauro, you don't even know what Mr. Cermak's correct job title was, did you? You got your information from those around you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Cermak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military governor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We'll come on to that in a moment. Did you know how many staff Mr. Cermak had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In your statement, you refer to his aides. Who did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were always soldiers around him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Because in fact he was the only interlocutor, if you want to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know about the structure that had been developed between the UN and the Croatian government whereby a liaison system had been set up and officers designated to assist with liaison work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I recall that in Zadar there was an office which had a civilian office, in fact, which was supposed to be our point of reference, and I also read the report, and I recall hearing our coordinator, that he was trying to set up a meeting for weeks and weeks, and then we finally managed to have a meeting after a few weeks or a few months - I don't remember, few weeks, probably - and I was present at that meet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In terms of the aides that you have referred to, are you in fact referring to liaison officers, for example, a Mr. Dondo, or a Mr. Lukovic? Do those names ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Probably 13 years ago, yes. Now, absolutely, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Had you ever met Mr. Cermak before he came to Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know when he was assigned to his position in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No, did you know when --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as far as I know, when I saw him. But I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you ever see the Croatian documents themselves assigning Mr. Cermak to his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And just for the sake of clarity, to come back to a question I raised earlier, it's right that you never saw any precise terms of reference as to what Mr. Cermak's actual job was, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Post-Operation Storm, were you personally given any formal instruction as to how the new civilian and military administration was to function in and around Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what I already said. We -- we knew that our point of reference was General Cermak and that the -- the civilian authorities were not yet in place and were to about be established, and then, I don't remember how many days or weeks later, Mr. Romanic came.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: My question is a very, again, specific one, Ms. Mauro, if I can come back to it. Were you given any formal instruction as to how the new civilian and military administration was to function in and around Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No more than what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, what you said before was that Mr. Cermak was a point of reference, which I don't disagree with. But my question was about formal instruction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we learned that in Zadar they were going to establish another point of reference for us, but no, it was very confusing, I must say, from this point of view. There was not clear -- clear idea on what was happening, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And building on that point you raised about confusion, is it fair to say that there was an element of confusion as to in fact who Mr. Cermak was and what his job was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, because in fact most of the people in the area were militaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: All right. Well, given your particular function and relatively limited time in the area by the events of post-Operation Storm, is it accurate to say that you were not familiar with the functioning and operating of the Croatian military structure post-Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a field of interest for UNMOs, not for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you would agree that you were not familiar with that aspect, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know how the Croatian military structure was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you didn't know how a garrison functioned in Croatia at that time, did you, Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a military person, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No. The reason I'm asking you this is because you feel able to make points about overall jurisdiction of individuals, so I'm sure you can understand that I'm asking to see the remits of your knowledge, Ms. Mauro. Now, the next question is: Either at the time or sometime thereafter, did you come to know that there was no such position in Croatia as military governor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: When asked by my learned friend to give the factors upon which you based your assumption that Mr. Cermak was the main authority in the area, you stated that it was "... undoubtful because within our own hierarchy the person we were relating to was him..." and that in fact, there was liaison between General Forand and General Cermak, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That's what you said, Ms. Mauro, so perhaps you can help me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that he was liaising formally with Mr. Forand and Mr. Al-Alfi, but that he was -- he was the only person who we could relate to. That's what I'm saying -- that's what I said, and that's what I repeat. There was nobody else we could relate to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The information that you had about his authority and his title was based on what you had been told by others within the UN. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your colleagues. Where did you get the information that Mr. Cermak was the governor of Knin from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was referred to as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you remember who told you that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not an information. He was called like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Within the UN?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We -- none of us was really speaking Croatian there, so I don't know if also Croatians would refer to them this way, but the interpreters used this translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you ever come to know that he was appointed in fact as the garrison commander and that was his correct title?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know he was a garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to now move to another topic of questioning, and I'd like to move to the issue of notification to Mr. Cermak about crimes that were happening in the area? Just so that you have a point of reference, Ms. Mauro, I'm going to first of all be looking at your 2000 statement, page 3 of that statement. On page 3 - I'll read it back to you - it states: "I know that Cermak and his aides were told on a number of occasions about killings, lootings and burnings of Serbian houses." Do you remember that part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
