utterances.text: And again, you know that because you were told that by others in the UN who were higher up than you who had the meetings with Mr. Cermak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Besides this few times we met, but then, yes. We were sharing information among UN people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You also say: "I recall Croatian officials there" -- on the same page -- "saying something like, it must be revenge for what has gone on before, and some of the people responsible are uncontrolled groups." Was that a common point of view at that time as to the cause of some of the crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the revenge was definitely one of -- one of the issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You didn't ascribe in your statement any particular Croatian official, and I presume that's to do so with the passage of time and you're unable to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct. I can remember there were some parliamentarian coming. There was a delegation of parliamentarian coming once. There was some Red Cross officials coming from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I want to move onto another part, and this concerns --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, may I seek some clarification of that last answer. You said you do not know exactly who told you, and then you give two -- you refer to two type of persons, parliamentarians, Red Cross people. Did you want to say it was either of the two or either some of the -- one of the parliamentarians or one of the Red Cross people, or did you want to say it was I heard it from one of the parliamentarians and I also heard it -- it's not clear for me what your answer was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly, but I remember that the revenge was one of the reasons that it was advocated for what was happening by parliamentarians. But you know, there was this big delegation coming in, and you would talk to someone in the outskirts. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You now use the plural "parliamentarians."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier also referred to the Red Cross. Did you hear it from one person, whether parliamentarian or Red Cross, or did you hear it from more persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from more persons, but I don't remember who they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I want to come onto, now, a specific example going back, again, to your 2000 statement, and if I may read it back to you so that you have it before you. The passage is the following: "I am aware that General Forand regularly complained to General Cermak, and I'm aware of a letter or report sent by Cermak to Forand, suggesting that the houses were not being burnt and that there was no problem." Do you recall that aspect of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Mauro, did you ever see the document that you refer to there yourself and the signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We know from your evidence in chief that on the 4th of September - and my learned friend referred to P36, which came up on the screen during your evidence - you were told that on the 4th of September, that Mr. Cermak was out of town. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall that we went through that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know or did you know at the time when Mr. Cermak left town, when he came back from town? Were you given that information at any point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You referred in your evidence in chief to the denial attitude, and that's something I want to briefly address with you now. In those debriefing sessions that were held with Mr. Al-Alfi, were you also made aware at that time of Mr. Cermak's position that crimes were indeed taking place and were labelled by him as a shame on Croatia? Did that come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I see if I can assist you by referring back to contemporaneous records of Mr. Al-Alfi's, because that might jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have D56, please, on the screen, and if I could have page 3 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Ms. Mauro, this is a UN report from Mr. Al-Alfi dated the 18th of August, and it's sent to Mr. Pavo Pitkinen [phoen] in the UN HQ in Zagreb, and he refers there to a meeting that he had that afternoon with General Cermak, and he refers to others who were present during that meeting. If you look at paragraph 2 on that page, it reads that: "During the meeting, I also brought to the attention of General Cermak our concern about the continuing reports of houses and farms set on fire in the villages and looting, and asked him about the measures taken from his side to stop such acts. General Cermak shared this concern with us and expressed his unhappiness about its continuation. He promised tough action against those who commit such acts. He also explained that some of the acts may be carried out by civilians who returned to the area and seek revenge, taking advantage of the lifting of restrictions on their movement in the area." Ms. Mauro, there is no aspect there, is there, of a denial attitude in respect of his response to Mr. Al-Alfi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was in this letter in September there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm asking you now about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- this document in context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D151, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just for the record, again, as the document is being pulled up onto the screen, this is almost a week later. Again, it's the same format of reports from Mr. Al-Alfi to the UNCRO HQ in Zagreb, and it's dated the 24th of August. On the first page, we see reference there to 1330 hours in the afternoon, General Forand had a meeting with General Cermak, meeting was held in the office of General Cermak, and the PHAC participated in the meeting. Now the PHAC was Mr. Al-Alfi; is that right? Civil affairs coordinator, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If this is from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I go to the next page, please, paragraph 5. Again, there, you see reference to the fact that: "We brought the continuation of burning houses and looting in the area to the attention of General Cermak and asked him to such" -- "stop", rather -- "such acts. He accepted this fact regarding the continuation of such incidents..." and you can read to whom he attributed them to if you continue to read the paragraph. I'm not going to read it all out to you. You can see there, there's reference by him to the fact that in his opinion the area is very vast, and he would be lying if he told us that nothing of this sort would continue to happen. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we were not understanding is why the strict orders were not reaching the people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Mauro, you're not able to assist me with the de facto, the factual authority that Mr. Cermak actually had, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro is telling us what came to her mind and, of course, she should not explore that. But, Ms. Higgins, she told us what they did not understand at the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is a personal observation, and she is entitled to include that in her answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And finally, if I could have onto the screen, please, D59. Ms. Mauro, during your time in Knin, as the document is coming onto the screen, were you able to access some of the Croatian media articles that were being published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I had time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. Was there someone there to assist with the translation of those articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. Can I ask to you look at this one in particular, which is an article from one of the main newspapers, Slobodna Dalmacija, and it's dated 7th of September, 1995. It's an interview with Mr. Cermak, and you can see the title there: "There is no place for looters in the Croatian army." And if you just read that article to yourself for a moment. Was that an article that came to your attention at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You can see that the article refers to the launching of operations to resolve problems there related to illegal appropriation of apartments, looting, and the torching of homes. Was it something that came up ever in those debriefing meetings, Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in our debriefing it came up the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this couldn't come up because, indeed, we were every day noticing that, unfortunately, it was continuing and that people were still in a very dreadful situation, and dead bodies were exhumed --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and found, elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, no, we didn't come to our debriefing up, unfortunately, that there were elements of substantial and determined action to stop what we were denouncing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you is, of course, because some of those reports were from Mr. Al-Alfi himself who headed up those debriefing meetings, so I'm trying to give you an opportunity to comment upon those.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may continue, probably we understood that there was a difference between facts and words.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, you've assisted me as far as you can with those reports. What I'd like to finally deal with with you is the issue of Grubori, if I can deal with it briefly. You have already explained to us and we've seen the report whereby you go and take your concerns to Mr. Romanic, you have a meeting with Mr. Romanic, and you ask him to come to a meeting with the local residents in the Plavno valley --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- which you set up to take place on the 25th of August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I guess he set up because we could have gone immediately, seen the conditions of the people there; we would have gone back straightaway. But we gave him, obviously, the opportunity to decide when it was more convenient to him, so he set the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And we know from one of your reports, the report that deals with this meeting, that it was proposed that both he and Mr. Pasic, who was the governor's commissioner, would both attend Plavno on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember Mr. Pasic. It's possible, but I don't remember Mr. Pasic in this moment. I remember Mr. Romanic. He would come, obviously, with someone else but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you take it from me, those are the names that are referred to in your own HRAT report; and if you want to see it, I'm sure you can be provided with a copy of it. It's P46.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not denying that Mr. Pasic wouldn't come. Would come, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you were present with a team on the 25th when you were visiting the hamlet of Zoric in the Plavno area, and that's when you saw smoke on the other side of the mountain whereby your team moved to travel to what we know to be Grubori, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it right that on that day, you were present with Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Romassev, member of UN CIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible. There was UN CIVPOL, but I don't remember his name. They were not always the same person, so they were rotating. So I don't remember everyday the name of every day --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Sure, I understand. Can you assist me with who else was there as a member of that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Was also someone from UNHCR. I mean, the person responsible for the UNHCR office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you remember the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yeah? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Olivier Mouquat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: How do you spell the surname, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: M-O-U-Q-U-A-T.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As international staff, I don't remember. Probably, there was also an UNMO. Most probably there was, but I don't remember. I remember these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now I want to ask -- sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. And also about Alun Roberts, I'm not completely certain, actually, about Alun Roberts. I'm not completely certain if he joined us after but ... yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about when you come to leave Grubori and you go back to Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You've told us from your first statement that that afternoon at 1630, "... we reported to General Cermak's office so they would respond but there was no response that day." Do you recall that part of your statement at page 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I repeat that there was another instance when we went, and there was no response, also, so probably was two times because it's -- what you are trying to ask me?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm only asking you to confirm that at 1630 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- on the 25th, you went to the office of Mr. Cermak as you call it, and you went there with who? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I told you already. I don't even remember if I was part of the team who went in the office of General Cermak that day. I remember that there was another instance, always in Plavno area, where I went, part of the team in General Cermak's office. But I do recall that part of the people who were with us did go to inform General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And is it right that none of those individuals who went actually spoke to Mr. Cermak himself? They, rather, spoke to a Mr. Dondo, who was one of the HV liaison officers. Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Right. So you're not sure whether you went into the building or you stayed outside. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not even sure whether -- because we were more cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not even sure whether I went to the office or I went directly to the headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can you help me with whether or not you were the individual who had a conversation with Mr. Dondo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm telling that I don't even remember that I went to the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about whether you recall a conversation, so you can help me with that, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said already no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether or not or can you remember whether the matter was reported that day by one your team to the police in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You can't remember, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I -- I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any knowledge about how crime investigations worked and functioned within Croatian society at that point, post-Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only what I was told about looting, for instance. It was not prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the responsibility of the crime police to investigate incidents that had taken place? Was that something within your knowledge as a patroller?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But we were not asked to refer to crime police. We never were asked to refer to crime police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about your knowledge of how the crime police worked. You understand, Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me the responsibility of the crime police, but we were not even aware that there was a crime police. So how we could know that they were responsible to investigate incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You had a meeting with Mr. Romanic. How many meetings with him did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't count them, and remember, 13 years later, surely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know who the commander of the Knin police station was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seemed him. He was -- at least he was the chief of police, then if there's a difference between commander and a chief of police, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you said that there was no response that day in respect of Grubori. Did it come to your knowledge ever that in fact the liaison officer that I have referred to, Mr. Dondo, went to Grubori the next day and provided information to the police in Croatia? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you go back to Grubori, Ms. Mauro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Because we saw these other houses burning, as I mentioned to you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you ever go in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not Grubori, sorry. We went to Plavno.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: To Plavno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But it was a valley, and all these villages, Grubori was, coming from Knin, was on your right side, and then you had Zoric, was on your left side, and then in the front you had more villages, so it was all a big valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you go back to the Grubori village or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was down, yes, where the school was, yes. Yeah, there were houses down in the valley. Yeah, I went there, but not up, up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: As you had been the one who had gone to bring the information to Mr. Romanic's attention and to set up the meeting, did you ever go back to Mr. Romanic to find out the reason why he was not there on the 25th at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am certain that knowing my professional morale, I did. I don't know if he had already left by then. This I don't remember, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What was his response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I mentioned, I don't know if he had already left by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I don't remember his response if there was one, but we were definitely astonished about what happened in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about is whether you went back and asked Mr. Romanic why he did not attend, and if you did so, could you give me the date, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't give the date now, but what I'm saying -- I just said, is that Mr. Romanic probably had already left, but I'm certain that we went back to the police to say, to inform what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Are you able to give me a HRAT report reference out of one of the 50 documents as to where I might find that record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because also if you notice, there is not everything written on what we had discussed with Mr. Romanic in the HRAT report, if you noticed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I did notice, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reading the report, yes. So were would just write -- we were investigating human rights. Then would have been a different report, and if there was something very important to -- to mention, would be in the HRAT. Otherwise, would not even be mentioned but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, it's not in the HRATs --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- which is why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So probably, we couldn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Higgins. Could I first of all inquire as to the time, Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably less than an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than an hour. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No more than 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the parties try? We have -- yes, it must be possible, therefore, to conclude the testimony of this witness today. Ms. Mahindaratne, could you give us any indication as to much time you would need in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question until now. Mr. Kuzmanovic, I think it would be best that you start the cross-examination because it would be a bit early for a break and then go on for another hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. I just need the lectern, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mauro, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, you were -- I just want to start where Ms. Higgins left off. You said, I believe, that Mr. Romanic, when you were referring to follow up with him, had left by then. You mean left -- left where? The Knin area by then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. He left suddenly. Again, I -- I apologise not having that good memory, but one day we went to see him, and we were told that he was not working anymore in Knin. He was transferred. And I don't remember exactly when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a HRAT report dated the 23rd of September, which is a little less than a month after the incident at Grubori where you indicate that you met with Mr. Romanic, the chief of police for the Knin area. So it had to be at that point in time he still had not left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. But he would also leave Knin for a while and then come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The point is that you yourself had never reported this incident at Grubori to Mr. Romanic, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't think it's correct. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me in what document that is it correct if there is a document that says something to that effect, that you, Ms. Mauro, or the HRAT reported this incident to Mr. Romanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that probably we reported to Cermak, General Cermak, and we thought that was most appropriate because the people, we saw them, were in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, if you read page 68, line 23, you see that the witness wanted to continue her answer. She said "but". "I don't think it's correct, but..." and then you interrupted her. Could you please allow the witness to finish her answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead. If you wanted to add something there, please feel free.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I think I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you meanwhile did, but I'm urging Mr. Kuzmanovic to give you immediately the possibility to finish your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appreciate it. It's very, very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- professional from you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The report that you wrote on Grubori was a three-day report, correct? It encompassed three days; it wasn't an individual report per day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P27. If we could pull that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is actually a four-day report encompassing the 24th through the 27th of 1995. Can you please tell me why there wasn't a separate report written for each day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good question. I think that we were really trying to work hard and to see how we could help these people and reassure these people, so we were most of the time out in -- in -- in the field, and could have coincided, also, with the arrival of some delegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was the time of the arrival of President Tudjman on the train, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of this report, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of this page, Ms. Mauro, there are three sets of initials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: EJ Flynn is the first, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Si.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then yours are the second initials, correct? MTM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Who is PS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Peter Soucek.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was this civilian affairs officer who was covering the area of Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And did the three of you put this report together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any input from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Well, there could have been input from military and the CIVPOL, but we would -- you know, security situation could have been -- any information we got from -- technical information we would get from militaries, yes. Could be possible then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: For this particular debriefing for which this report was written, can you recall, other than the three of you, the names of anyone else who may have participated in this writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nobody else would have participated. Again, we would have received information of technical military nature or others by CIVPOL, but -- sorry, UNMOs, military but -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mauro, I ask, please, if you would let me finish my question, and I will let you finish your answer. Thank you. You'll notice on the first page of P27, if we could go to P27 on page 1 of this same document. Paragraph 2, the first full paragraph, the bold section where it says: "Late update." Now, the late update on the 27th -- and I'll read from the -- the bold section. It says: "A HRAT which travelled to Grubori on the afternoon of 27 August has received reliable reports of a group of ten camouflage-clad Croatian special police moving up the road to Grubori mid-morning on 25 August." My question to you is, Were you aware or was anyone on your team aware that the Croatian special police never wore camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the army of the Republika Srpska military forces most often wore camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P46, please. Before we get to P46, were you aware that after Operation Storm into late August/early September, there were groups of ARSK soldiers in the woods, in the various areas north and east and south of Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware there were some ARSK soldiers who called in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And these were groups of soldiers that were hiding out in the woods, and do you know that one of the purposes of the mop-up operations was to find these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I also know that some of them basically asked us to facilitate their release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we did. In a couple of instances, I was personally involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'd like you to answer my question, which was ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you to have to look for your question, then maybe there was not one, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic asked whether you were -- whether you knew that one of the purposes of the mop-up operations was to find these individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P46, which is the 23rd of August, 1995, HRAT report, on the last page of this document, which is a three-page document, there are your initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I think you had mentioned earlier in your testimony that if your initials were on a document, you had participated in putting the document together, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I -- in this case, I guess I wrote the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. This is a document that you wrote, P46, from what your understanding is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can read --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. If we want to go back to the first page, and if you'd like to take a look at the document to confirm that, that would help, if that would help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, have you looked at the screen a second ago? Please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we go back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. If we could go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, if we do not make a small pause between question and answer, the transcriber cannot follow us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also try to assist us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, since we both speak the same language and the back-and-forth is a natural event of my questioning and your answering, sometimes my speed and your speed makes the translation not be able to stay with us, so ... It has nothing to do with the skill of the transcribers or the interpreters. Please feel free to take a look at this document, and if there's anything in there... We had discussed this document -- you had discussed this document with Ms. Higgins. You remember participating in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I called for this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you take a look at page 2 of this document, you've got in section 6: Mr. Jukic joined the meeting. And you were made aware -- or participants in the meeting were made aware that: "... a collection of dead human bodies is being carried out by a specialized team operating in the Knin area. According to him, this team is composed of one doctor, one burial specialist, and one criminal investigator." Now, knowing this from your meeting on August 23rd of 1995, is there a reason why you did not go to Mr. Romanic and ask for this type of team to come to Grubori?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again, I thought we were under the impression that General Cermak would have helped us in Grubori, in particular, because there were people in uniform, military uniform when we were there, so we thought that by informing him he would, as responsible, anyway, and the authority in Croatia, we were an international organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to point 8 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The document further says: "Mr. Jukic, along the line adopted by Mr. Romanic, invited UN representatives to direct reports relating to the dead bodies detected in Sector South to the civil defence."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, go ahead if you have a comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is, so you're specifically being directed - meaning UN representatives and international people, I would assume - to direct any information that you have regarding dead bodies directly to the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what we did, and the dead body of two or four people, I remember, remained lying in the village not far from Knin for days and days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we had informed, as I suggested, the civilian defence, but we saw that we didn't really succeed in removing these dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. This is four days before -- two days before Grubori, though, correct, you're being told this? Grubori was the 25th of August, and this meeting was the 23rd of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that these bodies we are referring to were after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. But at least as far as Grubori was concerned, you did not follow the suggestion here by Mr. Jukic and Mr. Romanic to report dead bodies detected in Sector South to civil defence, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: My statement is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't go to see Mr. Jukic in that precise instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Or Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Romanic, I think we did go, not immediately, but we did inform him on what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you yourself go back to Grubori the same day after you came back to Knin, meaning you went to Grubori, came back to Knin, and then went to Grubori the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. -- did anyone from your group stay in Grubori the entire time and come back later that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not certain, but if I recall correctly, someone did go in the afternoon, after -- went back. There was movement --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe my question wasn't clear enough. Was there a group from your group that went to Grubori that day that stayed when another portion of your group came back to Knin in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember if they stayed or if they came back and then they returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, one of your reports talks about the surrender of 14 RSK members, 12 miles -- or 12 kilometres from Knin, not too far from Plavno. I will find that report in a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But not too far from Plavno is your assumption or...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will get to that in a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before I get to P48, were you aware of any other instances of ARSK fighters either surrendering or being captured by any Croatian military forces before this particular report of the 28th of August that we're referring to in P46?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Or P48? Okay. P48 is dated on the cover page of 29th of August, 1995. If we go to the next page of that document, please. Were you present at this surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I was present when the RSK soldiers, so-called RSK, decided to surrender. I went up to this village to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go -- when you talked to them, was this a more than one-day event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to -- do you know of anyone else that might have gone there a day or two earlier to talk to these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I know is that just a few hours before, I went -- I had gone, the military observers or military, and that's why I went, because they wanted us to deal with -- with the matter and to involve, also, the Red Cross and to be certain that we would have the right liaison between military and civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Ermolaev involved in this? Does that name ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How about Mr. Tchernetsky?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was with me a police -- a civil police officer. There was also an UNMO, and there was also the national officer of the human rights centre for -- Centre for Human Rights, and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I realize it was a long time ago, but do you recall the names of any of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Probably the interpreter but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't want you to guess.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Probably, because they could have about two, one or the other, but I still don't want to say the names in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If at any point, Ms. Mauro, you have hesitation when referring to other people, to give their names, and if you would feel comfortable to do that in private session, you always may address me, and of course, it also depends on to what extent the parties are really seeking those names, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for purposes of this, I would just suggest we go briefly into private session, just if we can get the names, and then we can move back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mauro, we will turn into private session. That means what you'll say is not on the public record. I just took the opportunity to inform you that this is a possibility, that even when you testify in open session that portions, especially where you have concerns about other people, can be given in private session. I do understand now that Mr. Kuzmanovic would like you to answer the question, also, with the details of the names. So we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the 30 Croatian special police soldiers that were in this report, were you present when they arrived on the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And there was some tension there, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But it ended up being defused, and the individuals were essentially taken into custody without any significant issue of any kind, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, they were not taken in custody that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What happened was that we discussed with the colonel, I guess, responsible for the group of 30 Croatian soldiers, and he spoke to them, and it was agreed that they could have surrendered and that they would have been guaranteed fair treatment in the prison, and we reassured them that we would have taken their names up, and indeed, we went to visit them in prison afterwards. But they were taken -- taken away one day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So that had to be some significant trust between both the Croatian special police and you to leave them there, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that there was trust among the three of us at the end, because it was a very tense situation in the beginning, and we could have been misinterpreted, but -- by both sides, but then it was explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And everything ended up working out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian special police did take weapons away from these ARSK fighters, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to P1100.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a 25th September, 1995, report, Ms. Mauro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of this document, there's a discussion about making arrangements to assist persons to get their Croatian documentation, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the fourth line, it says -- the full sentence says: "The rest of people have to apply in Gracac municipality, while others, which were previously registered in areas where the registration books have been burned or lost, were only enlisted by the police." Now, my first question to you is, what do you mean by "only enlisted by the police"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were not provided with documents, and there was no record of who they were, where they were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware in many areas of the RSK in Sector South that the local Serb population either destroyed or took the birth registration and citizenship registration documentation with them when they left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I know that documents of this kind were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How they were missing, you're not certain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You had mentioned -- the last paragraph of this report you had talked about in one of your statements, Ms. Mauro, and that's your discussion with Mr. Barisic who was the coordinator for the Gracac area from the Ministry of Interior. There's some discussion here from Mr. Barisic where he says that the area was difficult to control because of its size being 200 square kilometres under the jurisdiction of Gracac, and that in the southern part of this area of responsibility, former HV soldiers and thus wearing uniforms were undertaking criminal actions and are particularly aggressive. It was also mentioned of bringing charges against 30 to 35 of them. Were you aware at the time, I guess, subsequent to your time spent in Croatia of how many persons were charged and/or prosecuted of either crimes of looting or any other kind of crime in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave Sector South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of 1995? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One last question for you, Ms. Mauro, or subject matter. You came in March of 1995 to Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were a civil affairs officer for the UN?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you -- you were based in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of March, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do up until the time of Operation Storm as a civil affairs officer in Sector South in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was looking after the well-being of the minority at that time, the Croatian population in -- in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go on patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, regularly, and I did my utmost to ensure that they would be taken care of, and I also mobilized the UN military, the medical teams of the UN militaries to provide assistance. I tried to facilitate encounters between the Croatian population living in -- in the sector and their family living in Croatia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to go into the Plavno valley area while -- before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mauro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Misetic, I'm wondering, perhaps, we could first have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, we'll have a break, and we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic. Ms. Mauro, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Going back to the previous examination, I also would like to draw the attention of the gentleman on a report dated 12 October 1995, where, indeed, we met civil defence representatives, but it was very difficult to understand who was doing what, and it's clearly specified that no one knew, really, who was this charge. So the reason why probably we did not -- we were not so strict in addressing the problem of dead bodies - besides the fact that they were not removed, they weren't done - was also that we perceived that the office was not working probably. So the report is dated 12 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to add that to your answer to the question put to you by Mr. Kuzmanovic about why you did not report this to Mr. Jukic or at least Mr. Jukic's service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Ms. Mauro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have Exhibit P62 on the screen, and if I could ask Mr. Usher to assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, in your 2000 statement, which is P1098, at page 2 towards the bottom, you mention when discussing the shelling, you say: "The shelling was intense, and we lived in a residential area with a school nearby, but I am aware that the school area did at some stage contain some military equipment." What I'm going to ask you to do is -- we'll show you an aerial map of Knin, and if you could circle and mark with an "A" the area where you lived, and mark with a "B" and circle the school that you're referring to. Can you orient yourself here on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with military aerial maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you look off in the right-hand part of the screen, you'll see the UN barracks, the Sector South headquarters. Do you see that? The UN camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you tell me which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the screen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- you'll see a see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- a circled -- or a blacked-off area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So does that help you orient yourself in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, especially if you indicate, please, where is the entrance?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be - let's see - on the -- if you look in the upper left-hand corner, you see where north is pointing. It would be on the north side of the UN compound, would be the entrance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Usher, could we -- we're not yet at the point where marking starts. Could you assist the witness by using the cursor on this screen. No, we cannot not follow what you point to the -- could you please come here and -- yes, there we are. Now, we have a -- yes, I was looking at the wrong screen. Could you first move the pointer so that we see the UN. That's the UN - from what I understand from the evidence until now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the UN compound, the entrance being, more or less, left-hand side of that. Now, if you would just move the cursor, Mr. Usher, a little bit down to the left, down to the left, following the road. That is the road that leads to Knin, and now up again to the right, so that direction, around Knin castle, and that's where you are approximately at the railway station. Are you able to orient yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relatively so. But I do remember that I was living in -- the school, at least, I was referring to was on the back of this main road. But how precisely far from either the main road and from the compound, I wouldn't be able to say from the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any other buildings that were in the immediate vicinity of where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The house was a two-storey house; and close by, there were these type of buildings, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, you know, I couldn't be precise. I can point -- can I use this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could point here, or I could point here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we just draw a big circle, Your Honour, in that general area?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, would it not be a good idea to help the witness, perhaps, a bit to tell her where you would cross the railway because that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, do you see the railway station that was just marked there, RRSTN?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you keep going north on that road, you would cross over. There's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: North is -- in order to avoid confusion, is to the left on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Keep going to the left. You would cross over a little bridge there, and then could you keep going up that road. Are you familiar with where the northern barracks is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Military barracks? No? Is the Tvik factory familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you find your way to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if we take the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from the railway station where the -- perhaps with the cursor we could -- Mr. Misetic, sorry. If you now move to the left, following the railway, there approximately you would cross the railway to enter into Knin town, and then I think -- no. I don't know who is moving it upwards now. If you would have crossed the railway, if you would go to the hospital, would you go ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would go -- my -- the residence where I was living was on the way to the hospital but in the back side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we move the picture in such a way that we also see the hospital. On this map, would you now be able to identify where the hospital is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm correct, it should be this way. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just try to -- if you would point at it with the cursor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Toward this -- this direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it in your hands now, Mr. Misetic, not to make it a co-production.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if that is correct, Ms. Mauro, does that help you now orient yourself on where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we pull the screen down a little bit so she can see the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The hospital is -- do you see the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could have been here or here. Oh, pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- there we go. Now, can you tell us the general area of where you believe you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in an attempt. Don't take it for granted, but it was -- it could have been somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you just draw a circle around the general area that you think you lived?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- given the witness's continuous, you know, expressions, saying that she cannot be certain, she's not sure, just a guesstimate, I don't know how safe it is to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's for the Chamber finally to determine how safe it is, and of course, we've heard all this, and we helped the witness to orient herself, and we are not unaware that there is still some hesitation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine for my purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, let me ask you, are you -- given that general area, are you able to find the school that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit number D955, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D955, map or aerial view marked by the witness, is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, on direct examination, you mentioned that your source, some of your sources for information in 1996 included, first of all, interpreters. Were these interpreters that you became reacquainted with when you went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both the ones I became acquainted with and the ones who remained in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me clarify that. You were in Belgrade in 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And once in Belgrade, were you receiving information about the situation in Croatia from interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and from - as I mentioned earlier - my landlady and her family and the friends of former UN national staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us who your landlady was? Was she someone who used to live in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you're asking for names, I wonder whether we do that in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will get as much information I can, and then ask for it in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic will take care of any possible concerns you may have. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to these interpreters, again, I wasn't clear on your earlier answer. Were these interpreters you were speaking with while you were in Belgrade? Were they former interpreters in UN Sector South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also in UN Sector North, because I worked in the UN Sector North north, as well, before going in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say friends of former UN national staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Friends and family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say UN national staff, generally, without giving me names, what are you referring to when you say UN national staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, they were interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So friends and family of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and of my landlady and from friends of friends. They had relatives in Belgrade, so these relatives in Belgrade would know people who were coming out of the exodus following 5th August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could move into private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going ask about one interpreter, Mr. President, but we've spoken about him publicly at length, so I don't think there is any need for private session. I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, were you familiar with an interpreter named Predrag Sare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what did you know about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a very competent interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When was the last time you spoke to him that you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I left Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or he left Knin. I don't remember, but ... since Knin, I never spoke to him anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to your fellow international colleagues in former Sector South, do you keep in contact with any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who you still keep in contact with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you -- can you tell us who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sajin Zhang. Olivier Mouquat. Igor Krnetic. Branka. Nina. Judith Jacob.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you keep in touch with Alun Roberts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alun Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Concerning Mr. Roberts, have you spoken with him at all about this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When was the last time you spoke to Mr. Roberts about this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw him here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the purpose of -- or what the circumstances were that had both you and Mr. Roberts here at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the date? Was it this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the last statement I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This would be January of 2008?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: January or February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. So can you tell us where you encountered Mr. Roberts while you were here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were sharing the same hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Roberts, was there anyone else here in The Hague when the two of you were here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Mr. Roberts while you were here in The Hague the events of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Briefly. But when you say who else was here, who else among who?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone from your time in Croatia in 1995 who was also present in the The Hague in January of 2008?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall what you briefly discussed with Mr. Roberts about the events in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we recalled a difficult moment that we went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that was the last occasion you spoke with Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you met with the Office of the Prosecutor in January, did you meet with them alone, or was Mr. Roberts present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, if I can show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have Exhibit D690.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in 1996 were you working at all with UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a document from October of 1995 that was -- a statement by Mrs. Sadako Ogata. I'm sure you're familiar with her, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could go to page 4 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph there or the paragraph that begins: "Secondly..." Mrs. Ogata stated that repatriation must take place in an organised phased manner. It goes on to talk about how adequate accommodation and essential services must be available in the places of return. It says: "Returning large numbers of refugees to areas which are not yet ready to receive them can have very serious consequences, not only for the refugees themselves but for the stability in the area concerned. I am thinking particularly of the still-fragile situation in the area of the Federation." Ms. Mauro, in your work with the UNHCR in 1996, were you aware that the issue of returns was actually one that involved multiple countries and repatriation of various refugee groups in order to be successful? Were you aware of how that process was unfolding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say -- you testified on direct about Croatians obstructing return. Was part of the issue the fact that these refugee return issues became interrelated so that return of refugees to Croatia was related to the return of Croatian refugees to Bosnia and -- et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But there were two issues, I think. One was the return proper, and the other one was the issuance of Croatian document, for instance, which was very slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kuzmanovic may have asked you this, but let me ask you directly. Were you aware that the underlying -- many of the underlying documents of the Croatian Serbs had in fact been taken to Belgrade as part of the "exodus" that you -- that is the word you used just a while ago, the exodus to Serbia on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is one of the interpretation. The other interpretation was that they were burned as soon as the Croatian authorities had come in, and I do not have an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, are you aware that in 2003 Croatia and Serbia reached an international agreement whereby Serbia officially returned all of those personal records back to Croatia? Are you aware of that now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, I have one question for you, and it's in relation to a question asked by Ms. Higgins. For the record, it's page 48, line 8, and just to remind you, Ms. Mauro, I'll read back the questions and answer. You were asked this question: "Is it right to say that from the brief contact that you had with Mr. Cermak in the UN compound that he was cooperating and trying to help out?" And you answered: "That's what I said. Then you were asked a question again: "Is it fair to say that given your position in Knin at that time, you weren't privy to the knowledge of what resources he had available to him or what he was authorised to do? It's not something that you knew about, was it?" And your answer was: "Well, he seemed to be the point of reference." And then you were asked this question: "My question is a bit more specific. In terms of whether you knew the resources he had available to him and whether you knew the authority he had to assist, do you see the difference?" And then you answered: "The resources, I don't know. The authority" - this is the answer that I would like you to focus on - the authority, it was stated because he wanted to be informed, and he wanted to, and he was reassuring. He was saying that the situation was under control, so and others were, I think also the chief of police referred to General Cermak, like, I can't really but General Cermak. That's what you have stated. That's what has been recorded, and that answer is not very clear? Now my question to you is: What did the chief of police say about Mr. Cermak which led you to draw certain conclusions about Mr. Cermak's authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he said that -- if I recall correctly, that General Cermak would have authority to influence the situation when it comes to problems with the looting, burning, criminal acts of all sorts, including killings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say chief of police, whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Chief of police, I'm referring to Romanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall when he said this to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one of our meetings when we were drawing his attention on the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to briefly set out the time-frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mauro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. I suggest that we first look at whether there are any questions for the Bench, and if then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Gwaunza has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, my question relates to a statement which is contained in your statement of 6 -- 5 and 6 January, 2008; that is it the supplemental statement, on the second page, page 2, paragraph 4. You refer there to an attempt to rescue some people, an attempt which was then stopped by the Croatian army, and this was -- this is alerting to people that you stated were stranded at a bridge or near a bridge. My question is, do you know what eventually happened to those people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, I would have a few questions for you as well. I'll just try to find them. Mr. Kuzmanovic asked questions about the meeting in which Mr. Jukic joined at a certain moment and explained to you -- explained to you about the teams with the doctor and the criminal technician, I think it was. And now, in that report, we find just after that portion where he invites you to report that Mr. Jukic explained that his team was slow because of false reports, where he said the reports were false because people killed were actually killed by Serbs, because they had refused to leave the area at the -- when the Croatian offensive started. Do you remember that this was said during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that there was something said about this, and it was also something said about why, for instance, a man and a woman would be buried together, because they would kill also the -- the woman if they would find a man. So there were such statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
