utterances.text: Yes. Did you form any opinion at that time on the basis of your own observations about the veracity of this statement, that people were killed by Serbs because they had refused to leave the area when the Croatian offensive started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because most of the people who were left were really elderly, and I think it would have been easy to kill all of them if this was the intention of the Serbs, if they were after killing people because they didn't want to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer started with no. I asked whether you formed an opinion about it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so the answer apparently is, yes, you formed an opinion about it, and the opinion was that you considered this to be a reasonable or did not consider this to be a reasonable explanation of the bodies being found being killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. In fact, I did form an opinion, and opinion was that if indeed it was true that people would be killed because they wouldn't leave the area, the killing would have been many more because most of the people who were there were elderly, and they could have killed all of them. So, no, I don't think that was done, because people didn't want to leave the area by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the information Mr. Jukic provided during this meeting, did that have any influence on your inclination to report or not to report dead bodies found to the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in what way did it influence your inclination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Biased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Now, you also explained to us that -- and you gave this as an addition to your earlier answer, that from a 12th of October, 1995, document, that you gained the impression that civil defence was not clear on their own tasks and -- now, I inform the parties that it's not yet in evidence, but I do understand that this is supposed -- that this is a reference most likely to 65 ter 596, which will be on your list from what I understand, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is a document called "HRAT Summary of Activities from the 6th to the 11th of October" dated the 12th of October. Ms. Mauro, you referred to this 12th of October document and the confusion. I read that document. Is that a document which refers to the meeting you had with Mr. Zlatko De Longa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Document of 12 October?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civil defence officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you told us that this may also have influenced you not to report but Mr. Zlatko De Longa, who apparently, according to this 12th of October document, creates quite a bit of confusion also following this report told that he arrived only two days prior to this meeting, which raises the following question for me: How could this lack of clarity on the civil defence apparently created by Mr. De Longa have had already its effect far before Mr. De Longa had arrived in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is just an additional evidence to corroborate our impression that the civil defence, in fact, either did not have information, either did not want to disclose information; and that impression was borne when I met Mr. Jukic the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. You answered a question about the information you -- that you had about the authority of Mr. Cermak and his title, and you were asked whether that information was based on what you had been told by others within the UN. When you were asked whether that was right, you answered: "My colleagues." Now, was it exclusively on the basis of the information given by your colleagues, or was your impression about the authority - I'm not talking about his title but just about his authority - was that based exclusively on what you had been told by others, your colleagues, or was it also based on your own observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both. But we worked as a team, and we all had the same impression, within the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But when I say your personal observation, I mean your personal observation in meetings with Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, my meetings were not official with Mr. Cermak, where in the compound it was not a formal meeting, but my impression was so, that he was an authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did it also include your observations or at least what you heard from Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Now, there's one question that was put to you that was about -- Ms. Higgins asked you about the position of the Croatian government concerning reintegration, and she asked you when she put this to you, she pointed at a document, and she asked you: "Do you see there an observation that Mr. Cermak stressed that Croatia does not want their town and wishes all these people to live there?" She said: "Do you see that, and did it come to your attention either at the time or shortly thereafter that that was in fact the position that Mr. Cermak had put forward?" Your answer was: "Well, yes." Could I verify with you the various elements of the question and then whether the "yes" applies to all the elements. She first asked whether you did see that it was the position, referring to the document, and may I take it that you saw that in the document that was put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the next part of the question was: "Did it come to your attention, either at the time or shortly thereafter, that this was in fact the position that Mr. Cermak had put forward?" Was your answer in the affirmative, also, on this element of the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that clarifies your answer. I have no further questions for you. Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just a couple of questions arising out of the clarification evidence that was elicited during my learned friend's re-examination. Further cross-examination by Ms. Higgins:

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, in relation to the conversation that you said that you had with Mr. Romanic about Mr. Cermak, we know that you met with Mr. Romanic on the 22nd of August. Now, you can take it from me that in that document, the record of your account, which is Prosecution Exhibit P46, there is no mention or reference to any such conversation there. There's no other HRAT report that I have been provided with that assists me as to when that conversation may have taken place. Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should look into the HRAT report, but may also not have been written.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's not in your statement, either, in fact, in either of your two statements. Is it something that you had told the Prosecution about during your proofing session or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you help me with any place that I might find a record of this conversation that you say took place concerning Mr. Cermak's influence concerning looting and burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if is written, then you may find in the HRAT report which refer to meetings with Mr. Romanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There are no such HRAT reports that contain such a conversation, Ms. Mauro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So may not have been written.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. During that alleged conversation, did Mr. Romanic tell you about the responsibility of the police to investigate crime and to stop crimes in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Romanic seemed really genuinely interested in helping, but he didn't, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Tell you about -- did he tell you about their responsibility, to investigate crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assumed that they have responsibility to investigate crimes as Ministry of Interior representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The question was simple. Did he tell you during this conversation that you had with him -- you say you had with him, did he tell you then about the responsibilities of the police? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, just for the sake of clarification as the word "meetings" has been used on several occasions, and just so that we understand each other, Ms. Mauro, would it be fair and right to say that you came across Mr. Cermak several times within the UN compound for no more than a few minutes at a time with others present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Kuzmanovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is borne out of your question, Your Honour, at page 102, line 10, or actually, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Mauro, Judge Orie asked you a question on the issue of the civil defence. The question was: "How could this lack of clarity on the civil defence apparently created by Mr. De Longa have already" -- "have had already its effect far before Mr. De Longa had arrived to the area?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could pull P46 up, please, second page, specifically paragraph 6, 7, and the first part of paragraph 8. Ms. Mauro, your answer to that question was: "This is just an additional evidence" - meaning your meeting with Mr. De Longa - "to corroborate our impression that the civil defence in fact either did not have information, either did not want to disclose information, and that impression was borne when I met Mr. Jukic the first time." Now, the first time you met Mr. Jukic was summarized in this report, P46; and in paragraphs 6, 7, and 8 of P46, he does provide you with information, and he doesn't fail to disclose any information to you, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: He provides you with the teams that the collection of dead animal -- dead human bodies is being carried out by a specialized team operating in the Knin area, and he describes what the team is for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: He also tells you how many bodies were buried in the Knin area. He also tells you that the records are submitted to the deputy prime minister, who was the only Croatian official authorised to speak to the public on this question, and he also invites UN representatives to direct reports relating to the dead bodies to be detected in Sector South to the civil defence. So he is providing you with information there, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And he's not failing to disclose anything to you in those two proves, is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you go probably down to the same document or in another document, you will also see that he is asking us to ask to the hospital about autopsies, and then we go to the hospital, and the hospital director doesn't want to talk to us or doesn't know what is, really, we are looking for, so there were contradictory evidences. Also --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Well, let's go to the -- let's go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can finish as you do. Thank you. Since he was talking about all this well-organised teams, which were cleaning the streets, removing dead animals and human bodies, that was not happening, in fact. So we were a bit reluctant to really take it seriously. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is nothing in this document summarizing your meeting with Mr. Jukic, which you said that your impression was borne of him when you met him the first time that says anything about the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you read the next report, you can see that dead bodies an animals, carcasses, and streets are not yet cleaning, and this happens for weeks and weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I would ask to you answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think in fairness to the witness, perhaps paragraph 8 can be read in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the point, of course, is that Mr. Kuzmanovic started referring to paragraph 6, 7 and 8, and later on he referred to the two paragraphs. I take it that you were referring to 6 and 7. Of course, the witness has answered some questions, many questions on this report. Ms. Mauro, if you would please take your time to re-read 6, 7, and 8 of this report, and then if you are done with most of 7, if you have to move to the next page, please inform us. And would you then, please, after you've done so, answer the question whether there's anything in this document which summarizes your meeting with Mr. Jukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you move to the next part of paragraph 8. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, four dead bodies in Zagrovic were not removed for many days after these, just one of the examples. And again, there is another report - I have not this good memory - to be asked to be pulled into the screen where I say that I go to see -- we go to see the director of the hospital in Knin because we were informed that they were responsible for autopsies, and there is no clear answer to who is responsible for the autopsies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions in this respect, Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In paragraph 8, and we can go back to that beginning portion of paragraph 8. The information that was provided specifically in paragraph 8, you did not do, correct, you would agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did. Zagrovic was one of the cases which is just in -- after paragraph 8. We reported about Zagrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You did not do that for Grubori, though, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because when I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that question was asked, was answered, and does not arise from the re-examination or the questions of the Bench, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Ms. Mauro, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again, wherever that may be at this moment. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Ms. Mauro out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to be here. It is more a responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties called you, Ms. Mauro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least the Prosecution, in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm just looking in the middle but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have got three minutes left. I know that there's a pending issue of expertise. However, I'm afraid that I will never be forgiven by interpreters and transcribers if I would give you an opportunity to start that debate at this moment, because it is not difficult to forecast what will happen, but it is that I have to apologise in ten minutes from now at the best for being late. I therefore suggest that any further submissions on that matter be made tomorrow before we start the testimony of the expert witness, Mr. Theunens, but we've got two minutes left to discuss whether this is a good suggestion. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi is here, Mr. President, for this reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's a good suggestion, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sure that the takee always thinks that's a good suggestion. I am a taker in the sense of -- with regard to the motion for prior drafts of the witness's report, that is certainly something we would want now, so the witness is due to begin tomorrow, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that a response would be filed today. I don't know whether this has been done, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. It's being finalised right now, and we will certainly file in next -- next couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you please take care that -- well, filing outside office hours is always a bit of a problem, but at least that you provide a courtesy copy to the Defence, and if you would forward it in such a way to the Chamber staff that we don't have to arrive tomorrow morning at -- too early to look at that, as well, and have an opportunity to look at it also this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think we always do that courtesy copies to the parties, including Chamber staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but of course, time and where to send it exactly so that we really are in a position to also read it this evening. That's a very practical matter, which, I take it, you will take up with the Chamber staff. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Obviously, there are some other issues, which we will defer until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's 7.00. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 19th of November, quarter past 2.00, in this same Courtroom I.
